title: How Well Do You Know Revelation?
subtitle: Test your grip on the Bible's final, vivid book.
about: Revelation is the strangest, most symbolic book in the Bible, and also one of the most hopeful: it ends with a wedding, a new city, and no more tears, not with defeat. Knowing it well means reading past the imagery to what it is actually promising.

verses.text: and he shall wipe away every tear from their eyes; and death shall be no more; neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain, any more: the first things are passed away.

questions.text: Who is traditionally named as the writer of Revelation, the one who received the vision?

options.explanation: Paul wrote many letters, but Revelation names its writer as John.
The book opens as the revelation given to John, the servant of God (Revelation 1:1).
Peter wrote two letters in the New Testament, but not Revelation.
Luke wrote a Gospel and the book of Acts, not Revelation.

questions.text: On what island was John when he received the vision?

options.explanation: Cyprus appears in the book of Acts on Paul's journeys, not in Revelation.
Crete shows up in Paul's travels and the letter to Titus, not here.
John says he was on the island called Patmos for the word of God (Revelation 1:9).
Malta is where Paul was shipwrecked in Acts, not where John saw his vision.

questions.text: How many churches are addressed in the letters near the start of Revelation?

options.explanation: There are more than three. The letters go to seven churches.
John writes to seven churches in Asia, like Ephesus, Smyrna, and Laodicea (Revelation 1:11).
Ten is too many. The letters are sent to seven churches.
Twelve fits the tribes and the apostles, but the churches here number seven.

questions.text: How is Jesus often pictured in Revelation, as a slain yet living animal?

options.explanation: Jesus is called the Lion of the tribe of Judah, but the slain figure is the Lamb.
The dove pictures the Spirit at Jesus' baptism, not the Lamb of Revelation.
John sees a Lamb that had been slain yet stands alive, worthy to open the scroll (Revelation 5:6).
An eagle appears among the living creatures, but Jesus is shown as the Lamb.

questions.text: How many seals are on the scroll that the Lamb opens?

options.explanation: There are more than three. The scroll has seven seals.
Five is short of the count. The scroll is sealed with seven seals.
The scroll is sealed with seven seals, and the Lamb opens each one (Revelation 5:1).
Twelve is a key number elsewhere, but the seals number seven.

questions.text: The four riders released as seals are opened are often called the Four Horsemen of what?

options.explanation: The four riders are commonly called the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse (Revelation 6:1-8).
The Exodus is the story of Moses leading Israel out of Egypt, not these riders.
That phrase does not name the riders. They are the Horsemen of the Apocalypse.
The covenant points to God's promises, not to the four riders.

questions.text: What did the angels sound to announce waves of judgment in Revelation?

options.explanation: Harps are played in worship scenes, but the judgments are announced by trumpets.
Seven angels were given seven trumpets, and each sounding brought judgment (Revelation 8:6).
Bells are not part of this scene. Seven angels sounded seven trumpets.
There are no drums here. The angels blew seven trumpets.

questions.text: What number is called the number of the beast in Revelation 13?

options.explanation: Seven is a number of completeness in the Bible, but the beast's number is different.
Revelation 13:18 gives the number of the beast as six hundred and sixty-six.
The number 144 connects to the sealed servants of God, not the beast.
The number 1260 marks a span of days in the visions, not the beast's number.

questions.text: What is the final battle named in Revelation 16, gathered at a place called by that name?

options.explanation: The kings are gathered to a place called Armageddon (Revelation 16:16).
Babylon is the great city that falls in Revelation, not the name of this battlefield.
Gomorrah was destroyed in Genesis, far from the visions of Revelation.
Jericho fell in the days of Joshua, not in the final battle of Revelation.

questions.text: What does John see coming down out of heaven near the end, prepared like a bride?

options.explanation: A throne is at the center of God's presence, but what descends is the holy city.
John sees the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down adorned as a bride (Revelation 21:2).
A mountain is where John is carried to view the city, but the city itself comes down.
The ark appears earlier in a vision, but the bride-like city is the new Jerusalem.

questions.text: In the new Jerusalem, what does God promise to do with every tear?

options.text: Wipe away every tear, with no more death or pain
options.explanation: Revelation 21:4 (ASV) says God shall wipe away every tear, and "death shall be no more."

options.text: Count every tear in a book
options.explanation: God knows our sorrows, but here the promise is that He wipes every tear away.
Tears do not remain. God promises to wipe them all away.
There is a river of life in the city, but the tears themselves are wiped away.

scoring.perfectMessage: You know the book of Revelation through and through.

gradeBands.message: A great reason to read Revelation slowly and carefully.

gradeBands.message: You know the main images of Revelation.

gradeBands.label: Interpreter
gradeBands.message: You know your way through this vivid book.

gradeBands.message: Remarkable. The visions of Revelation are clearly familiar to you.
